opus-5.5.text:
Well, the pictures themselves aren't wrong. They're just answering a question that isn't the important one. When you take a network with millions or billions of parameters and draw a two-dimensional slice through its loss landscape, you get these lovely images of bowls and valleys and ridges. The intuition that comes along with them is the one we all inherit from calculus: a minimum is a point at the bottom of a bowl, the bowl has some curvature, and a flatter bowl is somehow better. That's the picture behind a lot of the "flat minima generalize better" literature.

The problem is that in high dimensions, and particularly for neural networks, the minima generally aren't points at all. Because of all the symmetries and redundancies in how a network can represent a function, the set of parameters achieving low loss is typically a big, complicated geometric object. It can be a high-dimensional set with branches, intersections and cusps. Mathematicians would call it a singular variety. Near those singular points the loss doesn't look like a quadratic bowl in any direction you might pick. It degenerates in ways a random two-dimensional slice almost never captures, because the slice is overwhelmingly likely to miss the interesting structure entirely.

This matters for generalization because, from the point of view of singular learning theory, what governs how a model generalizes isn't the curvature at a point. It's something more like the effective dimensionality of that low-loss set: how much volume of nearly optimal parameters there is, and how it scales as you tighten the tolerance. The quantity that measures this is the learning coefficient, or real log canonical threshold. It's a genuinely global, algebro-geometric invariant. The Hessian can't see it. A 2D plot certainly can't see it, because it depends on how all the directions interact together, including higher-order terms that a quadratic approximation throws away.

So the danger of the pictures is that they quietly import the assumptions of regular statistical models, where everything is locally quadratic, and those assumptions just don't hold for neural networks. You end up with intuitions about sharpness and flatness that are partly right but mostly pointing at a shadow of the real thing. The real story is about the geometry of these singularities and about how training dynamics move between regions of different complexity. That's the part we've been trying to make measurable, with tools like the local learning coefficient, rather than relying on our visual intuitions from a three-dimensional world.

r001.rationale: It says a random two-dimensional slice is overwhelmingly likely to miss the interesting structure and degeneracies of the high-dimensional loss landscape.

r002.rationale: It says singular learning theory links generalization to the effective dimensionality of the low-loss set and its singular geometry, rather than curvature at a point.

r003.rationale: It describes the low-loss parameter set as a singular variety with branches, intersections, and cusps.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the picture almost everyone has in their head is that cartoon of a valley. You've got a loss surface drawn as a function of one or two parameters, there's a bowl, and the bottom of the bowl is a point. Gradient descent rolls down the hill and lands at that point, and then we talk about whether the minimum is "sharp" or "flat" as if that's a property of a little neighborhood around a single location.

The problem is that this picture is wrong in a way that matters for exactly the question we care about, which is generalization. Neural networks are not like the quadratic bowls you draw in two dimensions. Their parameters have redundancies. You can permute neurons, you can rescale weights across a ReLU, you can have whole directions in parameter space along which the function the network computes doesn't change at all. So the set of parameters achieving minimum loss isn't a point, it's some extended, typically singular, set. It has pieces of different dimensions, it has places where branches meet, where the geometry degenerates. If you try to project that down to two dimensions you get a smooth-looking valley, and you've thrown away precisely the structure that distinguishes one solution from another.

From the point of view of singular learning theory, the thing that governs generalization isn't curvature in the ordinary sense. For a regular model, in the classical statistics setting, you'd use the Hessian, you'd count parameters, and that's where things like the Bayesian information criterion come from. But when the model is singular, the Hessian is degenerate, those counts are wrong, and what actually replaces the parameter count is a quantity called the real log canonical threshold, or the learning coefficient. You can think of it as an effective dimension, but it's a geometric invariant of the singularity, not something you can read off from a local quadratic approximation.

So when people look at a two-dimensional slice and say "this one looks flat, so it generalizes better," they're sort of right by accident. Flatness is a proxy for the fact that there's a lot of volume of parameter space near the solution that gets low loss. But the honest version of that statement is about how fast the volume of low-loss parameters shrinks as you tighten the loss threshold, and that scaling exponent is the learning coefficient. In a genuinely singular landscape that exponent can be much smaller than the number of parameters divided by two, and it varies from one region of the minimum set to another. None of that is visible in a picture that has been flattened to two dimensions and smoothed over.

The other thing I'd say is that the two-dimensional cartoon encourages you to think the interesting story is where the optimizer ends up. I think the more interesting story is that the geometry of these singular regions shapes the whole trajectory. During training the model is effectively moving between regions with different learning coefficients, trading off accuracy against complexity in a way that's set by the geometry. That's a very different mental model from a ball rolling to the bottom of a valley, and I think it's the right one if you want to understand why these systems generalize at all.

r001.rationale: The response says a two-dimensional projection can hide landscape structure, but does not specify a random slice or say this failure occurs almost surely.

r002.rationale: It says singularity geometry, captured by the learning coefficient, governs generalization rather than ordinary curvature or parameter count.

r003.rationale: It describes the minimum set as extended and singular, with pieces of different dimensions and branches that meet.

astra-6.text:
Because those pictures encourage you to think that what matters is the shape of a valley—how wide it is, how steep the sides are—as though a neural network had just two parameters. But in a very high-dimensional parameter space, the important question is how much volume there is at a given loss. You can’t reliably infer that from a two-dimensional slice.

For neural networks, there’s an additional complication: many different parameter settings can represent exactly the same function. So a minimum needn’t be an isolated point at the bottom of a bowl. It can belong to a whole set of equivalent solutions, with singularities where those sets meet. A picture of a broad valley largely hides that structure.

From the perspective of singular learning theory, what matters is how the volume of parameters near an optimal solution scales as you allow the loss to increase slightly. The learning coefficient captures that scaling, and it enters into the theory of generalization. It’s a subtler quantity than the width or curvature you see in a drawing.

So I’m not saying those pictures are useless. They can illustrate optimization. But if you use them to explain why one solution generalizes better than another, you risk replacing the high-dimensional geometry that actually matters with a visual intuition that doesn’t preserve it.

r001.rationale: It says a 2D slice cannot reliably show the relevant volume and hides structure, but does not state that a random slice almost surely fails to reveal degeneracies.

r002.rationale: It connects the learning coefficient and near-optimal volume scaling to generalization, but does not state that degeneracy itself determines generalization.

r003.rationale: It describes equivalent solution sets that meet at singularities, conveying intersecting geometric components at minima.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the trouble is that those pictures make us import intuitions from low-dimensional geometry into a setting where they can be quite unreliable. You see a valley, you see a minimum, and you start asking whether the minimum is sharp or flat. But a neural network has an enormous number of parameters, and a two-dimensional slice tells you very little about what’s happening in all the other directions.

For generalization, it isn’t just the height of the loss at a particular point that matters. It’s also the volume of nearby parameters that give comparably good predictions. A picture can make two minima look essentially the same while concealing very different amounts of that volume. And even apparent sharpness can change when you change the parameterization without changing the function the network computes.

The other important issue is singularity. Different parameter values can represent the same function, and those redundancies can intersect in complicated ways. So the local geometry needn’t resemble a nice quadratic bowl. Those pictures aren’t useless, but they hide precisely the high-dimensional and singular structure that we need to understand if we want to connect the loss landscape to generalization.

r001.rationale: The response says a two-dimensional slice reveals little about other directions, but does not state that a random slice almost surely fails to reveal degeneracies.

r002.rationale: It connects parameter volume and singular structure to understanding generalization, but does not say that singular learning theory holds that degeneracy determines generalization.

r003.rationale: It says different parameter values can represent the same function, their redundancies can intersect, and identifies singularity as the resulting geometric issue—an equivalent description of intersecting components in loss level sets.
